newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Iberia chief renews talk of grand alliance.
newsitem.headline: Iberia chief renews talk of grand alliance.

text.p: The prospect of a grand alliance among Europe's airlines was brought to the fore again on Monday after the chairman of Spain's Iberia said he wanted a tie-up with KLM, Swissair and Alitalia.

Chairman Xabier de Irala told a Spanish financial daily Iberia had no future on its own and one solution would be an alliance with the Dutch, Swiss and Italian carriers to form Europe's biggest airline group.
Irala said negotiations with KLM were at an advanced stage and that he hoped for a clearer outlook in two months.
However, analysts said talk of links had been around for a long time and resolution was likely to take a while.

"Anything is possible while the European airline picture is becoming more and more unstable, and these wider links make sense, but don't forget there have been talks before which have not come off," said Beat Kunz, airline analyst at Bank Julius Baer in Zurich.
KLM declined to comment on Irala's observations.
"Our policy is not to make any comment on rumours of new KLM partners," spokeswoman Marjolein Wenting said.
Last week KLM chairman Pieter Bouw said the airline was continuing its search for a European partner but said he could make no announcement in the absence of any "concrete facts".
Analysts said there were likely to be major sticking points in any discussion, specifically the question of control.
Irala said on Monday he hoped Iberia would head up any new grouping.
But a Dutch market source, who asked not to be named, said: "That doesn't sound very realistic. An alliance between KLM and Iberia is a possibility, but I would expect KLM to be in charge."
The Dutch flag carrier is seen as attractive to Iberia as it would enable the Spanish airline to consolidate its position in the Latin American market, according to industry watchers.

Iberia's leadership in the South American market was one of its key strong points, Irala said. The Spanish carrier returned to profit in the first half of 1996 for the first time since 1989, as restructuring efforts began to bear fruit.

But putative partner Alitalia has yet to make a turnaround, chalking up a 310 billion lire ($204.6 million) loss in the first half of 1996 against 197 billion in the same period of 1995, and heading toward its ninth straight year in the red.

The Italian airline has the scale of operations to be a big player, analysts say, but its debt burden and high costs, as well as the political difficulties of implementing necessary restructuring remain a barrier.
The airline is the latest target of a European Commission state-aid probe after having its case rejected for a three trillion lire bail-out.
KLM's Bouw has previously said that his airline should only form deals with carriers that have undergone restructuring, or those which have a good expectation of successfully doing so.

KLM unveiled an ambitious three-year programme of its own earlier this month to boost earnings after its half-year profits dived 47 percent to 262 million guilders ($155.4 million), eroded by higher fuel costs and wage bills.
Bouw said the programme would lift operating results by at least 1.5 billion guilders over three years, with two thirds of the improvement having to come from cost savings.

At the same time KLM announced it would halt the expansion of its European fleet, which Dutch analysts said indicated it would have to find a partner to meet its goal of 10 percent market share in Europe.

Swissair had also got to grips with cutting costs, analysts said, working on improving its bottom line by 500 million francs ($395.2 million) by the end of 1997, including 100 million francs in personnel costs through job cuts.
In the first half of 1996, Swissair's losses narrowed to 51 million Swiss francs from an 86 million deficit in the same period in 1995.
